<reason>Side B (PRO) prevails by reframing the motion as demanding investigative scrutiny rather than automatic liability, and by establishing that knowingly pooling private data into a shared algorithmic "hub" constitutes concerted action through a common agent. Side B effectively neutralized Side A's "independent discretion" defense by noting cartel members also retain technical freedom to cheat, and exposed the circularity in requiring proof of coordination before permitting scrutiny when the relevant evidence sits inside platform contracts. While Side A offered a strong doctrinal defense of the conscious parallelism/agreement distinction, Side B better captured the functional equivalence between algorithmic and traditional cartels and the policy stakes of the "as if" framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.1-B4.5), particularly the answer that "communication runs through the hub by design" constituting the meeting of the minds on pricing method, and the argument that shared use creates the predicate for scrutiny rather than requiring proof of collusion as a precondition to investigation.</best_rebuttal>
